cues.text: A Nobleman's Sudden Renunciation
Born in 1090 at Fontaines, near Dijon in Burgundy, Bernard belonged to a family among the highest ranks of local nobility.
He received an excellent education and showed early promise as a scholar and writer.
At twenty-two, he resolved to enter the strict new monastery of Cîteaux , recently founded to restore the primitive austerity of Benedictine life, stunning his family and social circle.
Bernard's power of persuasion proved extraordinary even before he had taken a single religious vow.
He convinced some thirty companions, including four of his own brothers and, eventually, his own father and widowed sister, to join him in this renunciation of the world.
A single young nobleman's conversion thus set off, in effect, the wholesale conversion of his entire family and circle.
Founding Clairvaux in the Valley of Wormwood

Barely two years after entering religious life, Bernard was sent by the abbot of Cîteaux to found a new daughter monastery in a remote, desolate valley known locally as the Valley of Wormwood for its harsh and unforgiving terrain.
There, in 1115, Bernard established what would become Clairvaux Abbey, governing it as abbot for the remaining thirty-eight years of his life.
Through the sheer force of his spiritual authority, he transformed a wretched valley into the mother-house of one of the most influential monastic reforms in the whole history of the Western Church.
The Mellifluous Doctor
Bernard's writings — sermons, letters, and above all his extended, unfinished commentary on the Song of Songs — combined theological substance with rare eloquence and warmth.
Composed as spiritual meditations on the soul's union with God, these writings earned him, from later generations, the title Doctor Mellifluus , the "Honey-Sweet Doctor."

His devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary ran especially deep, and centuries of Marian piety bear the lasting imprint of his tender, theologically serious Marian spirituality, including some of the Church's most treasured Marian prayers traditionally associated with his name.
Healing a Divided Papacy
A disputed papal election in 1130 split Christendom between two rival claimants.
Bernard threw the full weight of his moral authority behind Pope Innocent II.
He traveled tirelessly across Europe to win kings' and bishops' support for the legitimate pope's cause.

His advocacy proved decisive: the rival claimant's support gradually collapsed, and by 1138 the schism had ended entirely — a peace achieved less by armies than by one monk's relentless letters, sermons, and personal persuasion.
Preacher of a Crusade That Failed

At the request of Pope Eugenius III, a former monk of Bernard's own Clairvaux, Bernard became the principal preacher recruiting support for the Second Crusade, drawing enormous crowds and securing pledges from kings and nobles across Western Europe.
The crusade itself ended in military disaster, a failure that grieved Bernard deeply in his final years.
In his own later writing, he struggled candidly to reconcile this with his confidence that he had been acting rightly in urging it.
Legacy
Bernard died at Clairvaux on 20 August 1153, having founded, over his lifetime, some one hundred and sixty-three monasteries across Europe.
By the time of his death, the number had grown to over three hundred, testifying to the extraordinary reach of the Cistercian reform he had done more than any other single figure to establish.
Canonized in 1174 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1830, Bernard remains a model of fierce reforming zeal and rigorous theological seriousness.
His genuinely tender devotion — to Christ, to the Church's unity, and above all to Mary — belongs, without contradiction, to a single life poured out entirely for God.
Few figures of the whole medieval Church combined so completely the reformer's uncompromising demand and the mystic's gentlest tenderness.
